subject: HEALTH
overview: Third-grade health is taught in short 20-minute lessons that pair one fact or skill with a hands-on activity at home: logging food, testing a helmet, practicing a 911 call or role-playing a refusal. Model each skill first, let the child practice it with you, then have them explain it back in their own words. Units on body safety, bullying, medicine, tobacco and alcohol should be previewed by the parent; keep the tone calm and factual and make clear the child can always come to you with questions.

weeks.prep: Print or open the MyPlate Kids page (myplate.gov); gather grocery flyers, scissors, glue and a paper plate divided into MyPlate sections (half fruits and vegetables, a bit more vegetables than fruit; grains and protein on the other half; dairy as a cup on the side). Prepare a simple food-log sheet with columns for each group.
misconceptions: Thinking a food belongs to only the group of its main look (e.g., pizza is 'grains'). Mixed foods count in several groups: crust = grains, sauce = vegetables, cheese = dairy, toppings may be protein or vegetables.
Thinking beans are only vegetables or that eggs are dairy. Beans and peas can count as protein or vegetables; eggs are in the protein group, not dairy.

days.guide: Look at the MyPlate Kids page together. Point to each section and have the child name it; then make a chart with the 5 groups and have the child write 3 foods in each. Check that every example is in the right group.

questions.q: What are the five MyPlate food groups?
questions.a: Fruits, vegetables, grains, protein and dairy.

questions.q: Name one food from the grains group and one from the protein group.
questions.a: Grains: bread, rice, oatmeal, pasta or tortillas. Protein: chicken, fish, beans, eggs, nuts or tofu.

days.guide: Have the child cut 15–20 food pictures from flyers and glue each into the right section of the paper-plate MyPlate. Ask them to justify any tricky ones (cheese, beans, juice) before gluing.

questions.q: Which group does cheese go in? Which group do beans go in?
questions.a: Cheese is dairy. Beans go in protein (they can also count as a vegetable).

questions.q: Which half of MyPlate should be filled with fruits and vegetables?
questions.a: Half of the plate should be fruits and vegetables, with a little more vegetables than fruit.

days.guide: Explain that nutrients are the parts of food the body uses, and give one job each: protein builds and repairs muscles, calcium builds bones and teeth, carbohydrates give energy, vitamins and minerals help the body work, fiber helps digestion, water carries things through the body. Child matches food cards to jobs.

questions.q: Which nutrient builds strong bones, and name a food that has it?
questions.a: Calcium; milk, yogurt, cheese, fortified soy milk or leafy greens.

questions.q: What is protein's job? Give a food with protein.
questions.a: Protein builds and repairs muscles and other body parts; chicken, fish, eggs, beans, nuts or tofu.

days.guide: Give the child the food-log sheet to fill in through the day (help with breakfast so they see how). In the evening, put a tally mark in each group for every food and add them up.

questions.q: Your sandwich had bread, turkey, lettuce and cheese. Which groups does it count for?
questions.a: Bread = grains, turkey = protein, lettuce = vegetables, cheese = dairy (four groups).

questions.q: Why do we keep a food log?
questions.a: To see what we actually eat so we can notice which groups we eat a lot of and which we are missing.

days.guide: Review the tallies with the child and have them circle the group with the fewest marks. They choose 2 foods from that group they would enjoy and plan when to eat them.

questions.q: Why does eating a variety of foods matter?
questions.a: Different foods give different nutrients; no single food has everything the body needs, so eating from all groups keeps the body healthy.

questions.q: If you ate almost no vegetables yesterday, name 2 you could add.
questions.a: Any two vegetables, e.g., carrot sticks at lunch and broccoli at dinner.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for the food log analysis: 4 = log is complete for the whole day, every food is placed in the correct group, servings are tallied for all 5 groups, and the child names the group eaten least plus 2 specific foods to add from that group; 3 = log is mostly complete with 1–2 sorting errors and a correct 'least' group with 2 foods; 2 = incomplete log or several mis-sorted foods, only 1 suggestion; 1 = log missing most of the day and no analysis.

weeks.prep: Measuring cup, a water bottle, 2–3 snack choices, a can of regular soda (or its label), white sugar, a teaspoon and a clear cup. Know the numbers: a 12-oz can of regular soda has about 39 g of sugar, which is about 10 teaspoons (1 tsp ≈ 4 g). Children about 8 years old need roughly 5–7 cups of water a day, more when active or hot.
misconceptions: Thinking juice and sports drinks count as 'just water.' They often contain a lot of sugar; plain water or milk are the best everyday drinks.
Believing skipping breakfast is fine if you aren't hungry. Breakfast refuels the brain and body after a night without food and helps focus and energy at school.
Thinking 'healthy snack' means 'no taste.' Help the child find snacks they enjoy that combine 2 food groups, like apple with peanut butter or cheese with crackers.

days.guide: Talk about how the body has been 'fasting' all night and breakfast is fuel for the brain. The child plans 3 breakfasts, labeling the food groups in each, and you check that each has at least 3 groups.

questions.q: Why is breakfast important?
questions.a: It refuels the body and brain after a night without food, giving energy and helping you pay attention and learn.

questions.q: Is 'oatmeal with banana and a glass of milk' a breakfast with 3 food groups? Which?
questions.a: Yes: grains (oatmeal), fruit (banana) and dairy (milk).

days.guide: Teach the decide-act-check steps: Decide (think of choices and what happens with each), Act (choose), Check (was it a healthy choice? would I choose it again?). Walk through chips vs. apple with peanut butter aloud, then the child does 3 more pairs.

questions.q: Chips or apple with peanut butter — which is healthier and why?
questions.a: Apple with peanut butter: it has fruit and protein plus fiber, while chips are mostly salt, fat and refined starch with few nutrients.

questions.q: What are the three steps of decide-act-check?
questions.a: Decide: think about the choices and results. Act: make the choice. Check: look back at whether it was healthy and what you'd do next time.

days.guide: Have the child fill a water bottle and record each cup they drink today with tally marks. At the end of the day, compare to about 5–7 cups and plan one time of day to add water.

questions.q: About how many cups of water should a third grader drink each day?
questions.a: Roughly 5–7 cups (more when it is hot or when exercising).

questions.q: Name two jobs water does in the body.
questions.a: It cools the body through sweat, carries nutrients, helps digestion, and keeps joints and organs working.

days.guide: Read the soda label: about 39 g sugar. Divide by 4 g per teaspoon to get about 10 teaspoons, and have the child spoon 10 teaspoons of sugar into a clear cup. Compare with water, which has 0.

questions.q: A soda has 39 grams of sugar. About how many teaspoons is that if 1 teaspoon is 4 grams?
questions.a: About 10 teaspoons (39 ÷ 4 ≈ 9¾).

questions.q: What is the healthiest drink to choose when you're thirsty?
questions.a: Water (plain milk is also a good choice at meals).

days.guide: The child designs a 'healthy snack menu' card with 6 snacks and posts it in the kitchen. Ask them to explain which food groups each snack includes.

questions.q: Give one snack that combines two food groups.
questions.a: Examples: apple + peanut butter (fruit + protein), yogurt + berries (dairy + fruit), cheese + whole-grain crackers (dairy + grains), carrots + hummus (vegetable + protein).

questions.q: Why is a snack with two groups better than one?
questions.a: It gives more nutrients and keeps you full longer.

weeks.assessment_key: Healthy snack menu rubric: 4 = card lists 6 snacks, each includes at least one fruit, vegetable, whole grain, dairy or protein food (most combine 2 groups), no more than one 'sometimes' treat, and it is neat and easy to read; 3 = 6 snacks, mostly healthy, 1 weak choice; 2 = fewer than 6 or several sugary/salty items; 1 = mostly chips, candy or soda.

weeks.prep: Three cereal boxes and two yogurt containers with Nutrition Facts labels. Preview the labels so you know serving size, sugar and fiber for each. Plan a short grocery trip for Day 4. Prepare 5 questions about one new label for Day 5.
misconceptions: Comparing whole-package numbers instead of per-serving numbers. All label numbers are for ONE serving; check the serving size first.
Thinking the first ingredient is the least important. Ingredients are listed from most to least by weight, so the first ingredient is what the food has the most of.
Assuming 'low fat' or a healthy-looking box means healthy. Always check the sugar, sodium and fiber numbers.

days.guide: Show a Nutrition Facts label and point to each part: serving size, calories, total sugars, sodium, dietary fiber. The child highlights each one on two different labels.

questions.q: Where on a label do you look first, and why?
questions.a: Serving size, because all the numbers on the label are for one serving.

questions.q: Which two numbers on a label should usually be low, and which should be higher?
questions.a: Sugar and sodium should be low; fiber should be higher.

days.guide: Make a table of the 3 cereals' sugar and fiber per serving. The child ranks them from healthiest (low sugar, high fiber) to least healthy and explains the ranking.

questions.q: Cereal A: 3 g sugar, 4 g fiber. Cereal B: 14 g sugar, 1 g fiber. Which is healthier?
questions.a: Cereal A, because it has much less sugar and more fiber.

questions.q: Why is fiber good?
questions.a: It helps digestion and helps you feel full longer.

days.guide: Read an ingredient list aloud and explain that ingredients go from most to least. Have the child find words that mean sugar (sugar, corn syrup, honey, cane juice, words ending in -ose) in 2 lists.

questions.q: If 'sugar' is the first ingredient, what does that tell you?
questions.a: The food has more sugar than any other ingredient.

questions.q: Name two other names for sugar on an ingredient list.
questions.a: Any two: corn syrup, high-fructose corn syrup, honey, cane sugar, dextrose, sucrose, fructose, molasses.

days.guide: At the store, the child picks one food (bread, yogurt or crackers) and compares two brands' labels. They choose the healthier one and give 2 reasons based on the numbers.

questions.q: Yogurt 1 has 18 g sugar; Yogurt 2 has 9 g. Same serving size. Which is the better choice?
questions.a: Yogurt 2, with half the sugar.

questions.q: Why must the serving sizes be the same to compare fairly?
questions.a: If the servings differ, the numbers aren't measuring the same amount of food.

days.guide: Give a new label and ask the 5 questions in the assessment. Let the child point to the line on the label as they answer.

questions.q: A label says 2 servings per container and 150 calories per serving. How many calories in the whole container?
questions.a: 300 calories (2 × 150).

questions.q: Does a big number for sodium mean the food is salty or sweet?
questions.a: Salty; sodium is in salt.

weeks.assessment_key: Food label quiz (5 questions on a label you choose): answers come from that label. Model key for a typical cereal label: 1) the serving size (e.g., 1 cup); 2) calories per serving (e.g., 140); 3) grams of sugar per serving (e.g., 12 g); 4) grams of fiber (e.g., 3 g); 5) the first ingredient = the ingredient it contains most of (e.g., whole grain oats). Scoring: 5/5 proficient, 4/5 approaching, 3 or fewer reteach how to locate each line.

weeks.prep: Two cereal boxes with cartoon characters or prizes; find 2 short food commercials on YouTube to preview (choose kid-targeted ones). Paper and markers for the ad.
misconceptions: Believing ads just give information. Ads are made to persuade you to buy; they show the best side and leave out things like sugar content.
Thinking that if a famous character or athlete likes a food, it must be good for you. Characters and celebrities are paid or used to make you want the product.

days.guide: Look at a cereal box with the child and hunt for 'tricks': cartoon characters, prizes, bright colors, words like 'fun' or 'power,' placement at kid eye level. List them, then check the label to see what's really inside.

questions.q: Why do cereal boxes for kids often have cartoon characters?
questions.a: To catch kids' attention and make them want the cereal, even if it is high in sugar.

questions.q: Name two other tricks on food packaging.
questions.a: Prizes or toys, bright colors, games on the box, health words like 'made with whole grain,' or celebrity pictures.

days.guide: Watch 2 commercials. After each, ask: Who is this for? What does it promise (fun, friends, energy)? What doesn't it tell you? The child records answers in a 3-column chart.

questions.q: How can you tell a commercial is aimed at kids?
questions.a: It uses kids as actors, cartoons, toys, games, music and fun or excitement instead of facts.

questions.q: What is something a food ad might leave out?
questions.a: How much sugar, salt or fat it has, or the serving size.

days.guide: The child designs a poster or storyboard that makes a vegetable exciting, using the same tricks ads use. Encourage a slogan and a true fact about the vegetable.

questions.q: What ad technique could you use to make broccoli appealing?
questions.a: Any: a cartoon character, a catchy slogan, bright colors, a promise like 'grow strong,' or showing kids having fun eating it.

days.guide: The child presents the ad to the family and names each technique and who the audience is. Family members ask one question each.

questions.q: Who is the target audience of your ad and how do you know?
questions.a: Answer names a specific audience (e.g., kids ages 6–9) and points to features aimed at them (cartoons, fun colors, games).

days.guide: Ask the child to write 3–5 sentences: how ads can change what kids want, and what questions to ask before believing them (What are they selling? What's left out? What does the label say?).

questions.q: What questions should you ask yourself when you see a food ad?
questions.a: Who made this and what are they selling? What is it promising? What isn't it telling me? What does the label say?

weeks.assessment_key: Healthy food ad rubric: 4 = ad makes a vegetable appealing using at least 2 named techniques (bright colors, catchy slogan, character, 'fun' or 'strong' promise) and includes 1 true health fact; the explanation names each technique and the target audience; 3 = ad and explanation with 1–2 techniques named; 2 = ad present but techniques not explained; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Activity log sheet and a timer. Know the guideline: children need at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day. Prepare a SMART goal template (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) and a 7-day tracker.
misconceptions: Thinking only sports count as exercise. Walking, biking, dancing, playing tag, swimming and chores like raking all count.
Writing a vague goal like 'exercise more.' A SMART goal says exactly what, how much and when: 'I will ride my bike 20 minutes after lunch 5 days this week.'

days.guide: Brainstorm with the child how activity helps: heart gets stronger, muscles and bones get stronger, better mood, better sleep, healthy weight. They draw a body and label 5 benefits.

questions.q: Name three ways physical activity helps your body.
questions.a: Any three: strengthens the heart and lungs, builds muscles, strengthens bones, improves mood, helps you sleep better, keeps a healthy weight.

days.guide: The child logs every activity and its minutes today. Add the total and compare to 60 minutes.

questions.q: How many minutes of activity do kids need each day?
questions.a: At least 60 minutes.

questions.q: You walked 15 minutes, played tag 20 minutes and biked 10 minutes. How many more minutes to reach 60?

days.guide: Track screen time for the day. The child lists 5 'active swaps' (instead of a show, dance to 2 songs; instead of a game, shoot hoops).

questions.q: Why does too much screen time make it harder to be healthy?
questions.a: Sitting a long time replaces active play and can disturb sleep.

questions.q: Give one active swap for screen time.
questions.a: Any active choice, e.g., a bike ride, jump rope, a walk, dancing or playing outside.

days.guide: Explain SMART with an example. The child writes a one-week SMART goal to add activity or a fruit/vegetable serving and sets up a 7-day tracker.

questions.q: Is 'I will be healthier' a SMART goal? Fix it.
questions.a: No, it is not specific or measurable. Example fix: 'I will eat one vegetable at lunch every day for 7 days.'

questions.q: What does the M in SMART stand for?
questions.a: Measurable: you can count or check it.

days.guide: Check day 1 of the tracker together. Ask what made it easy or hard and plan 2 supports (a reminder, a family helper, putting fruit on the counter).

questions.q: What is a 'support' for a goal?
questions.a: Something or someone that helps you reach it, like a reminder, a family member who joins you, or setting things up ahead of time.

weeks.assessment_key: SMART goal and tracker rubric: 4 = goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound (e.g., 'I will play outside for 30 extra minutes every day this week'), tracker has 7 days with daily checks, and child lists at least 2 supports; 3 = goal missing one SMART part; 2 = vague goal but tracker started; 1 = no clear goal.

weeks.prep: A simple recipe for the planned dinner, kitchen tools, and grocery money or flyers for price estimates. Review kitchen safety: wash hands, adult handles knives and hot stove/oven, pot handles turned in. Prepare the Unit 1 quiz below.
misconceptions: Thinking a balanced meal needs exactly equal amounts of every food. MyPlate shows about half fruits and vegetables, a quarter grains and a quarter protein, with dairy on the side.
Forgetting food safety while cooking. Wash hands before and after touching raw meat, and use separate cutting boards for raw meat and produce.

days.guide: The child plans a dinner for the family that includes all 5 food groups, drawing it on a MyPlate outline and labeling each food's group.

questions.q: Plan a dinner with all 5 groups.
questions.a: Example: baked chicken (protein), brown rice (grains), green beans (vegetables), sliced oranges (fruit), a glass of milk (dairy).

days.guide: The child writes a shopping list for the meal with quantities and uses flyers or a store website to estimate each cost and the total.

questions.q: If chicken costs $8, rice $3 and green beans $2, what is the total?

days.guide: Cook together. Before starting, the child lists 3 kitchen safety rules; supervise any knife or heat use.

questions.q: Name three kitchen safety habits.
questions.a: Wash hands with soap first and after touching raw meat; an adult handles hot stoves and sharp knives; turn pot handles inward; wipe spills; use oven mitts.

questions.q: Why use a different cutting board for raw chicken and vegetables?
questions.a: Raw chicken can carry germs (like salmonella) that could spread to food that won't be cooked.

days.guide: The child makes a 'Eat a Rainbow' poster with fruits and vegetables of different colors and one sentence encouraging the family.

questions.q: Why eat fruits and vegetables of many colors?
questions.a: Different colors have different vitamins and nutrients, so eating a variety gives the body more of what it needs.

days.guide: Review the goal tracker, then give the Unit 1 quiz orally or written.

questions.q: What did your goal tracker show? What would you do differently?
questions.a: Answer should cite the number of days the goal was met and name one specific change.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 quiz key: 1) Five food groups: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy. 2) Half the plate should be fruits and vegetables. 3) Look at serving size first on a label. 4) Ingredients are listed from most to least. 5) Kids need 60 minutes of activity daily. 6) A drink with 0 g sugar: water. 7) One ad trick: cartoon characters/prizes/bright colors. 8) Calcium builds bones. Meal plan: proficient plan includes all 5 groups with a named food for each. Goal tracker: proficient = at least 5 of 7 days recorded with an honest reflection. 7–8 correct = proficient.

weeks.prep: Clean a chicken drumstick bone (boil and scrub off meat), a jar and vinegar; start the soak on Day 2 and check on Day 5 (after about 3 days). A skeleton/muscle diagram to label. A book to lift.
misconceptions: Thinking bones are dead, dry and unchanging. Living bones are growing tissue with blood vessels; they repair themselves and need calcium and exercise.
Thinking muscles push. Muscles can only pull; that's why they work in pairs (biceps pull the arm up, triceps pull it straight).

days.guide: Point to the skull, ribs, spine and femur on a diagram and on the child's body, and say what each protects or does. Explain bones store calcium and need it to stay hard.

questions.q: What does the skull protect? What do the ribs protect?
questions.a: The skull protects the brain; the ribs protect the heart and lungs.

questions.q: What is the longest bone in your body?
questions.a: The femur (thigh bone).

days.guide: Place the clean bone in a jar of vinegar and have the child predict what will happen. Record a 'before' drawing and how it feels (hard, stiff).

questions.q: Predict: what will vinegar do to the bone?
questions.a: The vinegar (an acid) dissolves the calcium, so the bone will become soft and bendy after a few days.

days.guide: Have the child bend their elbow and knee (hinge joints: back and forth) and swing their arm and leg in circles (ball-and-socket at shoulder and hip). They list where each joint type is.

questions.q: Where are ball-and-socket joints? What movement can they do?
questions.a: Shoulder and hip; they can move in circles and many directions.

questions.q: What kind of joint is your elbow?
questions.a: A hinge joint; it moves back and forth like a door.

days.guide: Have the child lift a book by bending the elbow while you feel the biceps tighten, then lower it and feel the triceps. Explain muscles pull in pairs.

questions.q: When you bend your arm, which muscle tightens? When you straighten it?
questions.a: Bending: the biceps contracts. Straightening: the triceps contracts.

questions.q: Why do muscles work in pairs?
questions.a: Muscles can only pull, not push, so one pulls a bone one way and its partner pulls it back.

days.guide: Remove the bone from the vinegar and let the child bend it. Then they label the skeleton and muscle diagram and list 2 ways to keep bones and muscles strong.

questions.q: Why did the bone become bendy?
questions.a: The vinegar removed the calcium, which is what makes bones hard.

questions.q: Name two ways to keep your bones strong.
questions.a: Eat calcium-rich foods (milk, yogurt, cheese, leafy greens) and do weight-bearing exercise like running and jumping.

weeks.assessment_key: Labeled diagram key: skeleton labels skull (protects brain), ribs (protect heart and lungs), spine/backbone (supports body, protects spinal cord), femur (thigh bone, longest bone), plus any other correct bones; muscles: biceps (front of upper arm), triceps (back of upper arm), and one more (e.g., heart, quadriceps). Two ways to keep bones and muscles strong: eat calcium foods (milk, yogurt, greens), weight-bearing exercise (running, jumping), get enough protein, wear protective gear. Proficient: 6 correct labels and 2 strategies.

weeks.prep: Zip-top bag, a few crackers, water, a 20-foot piece of string or yarn, and a digestive-system diagram (KidsHealth has a kid version).
misconceptions: Thinking food goes straight from the stomach out of the body. Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine; the large intestine absorbs water before waste leaves.
Thinking digestion starts in the stomach. It starts in the mouth with chewing and saliva.

days.guide: Trace the path on a diagram with the child's finger: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. Say one job for each.

questions.q: What is the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach?
questions.a: The esophagus.

questions.q: Where does digestion begin?
questions.a: In the mouth, where teeth chew and saliva starts breaking food down.

days.guide: Put crackers in a zip bag ('teeth' crush them), add water ('stomach juices'), seal and squish ('stomach muscles churn'). Discuss what it models.

questions.q: What did squishing the bag represent?
questions.a: The stomach's muscles churning and mixing food with digestive juices.

questions.q: What did the water represent?
questions.a: Saliva and stomach juices that soften and break down food.

days.guide: Lay out a 20-foot string in a hallway or yard and talk about how the small intestine is coiled to fit in the belly. Explain that nutrients pass into the blood here.

questions.q: About how long is the small intestine of an adult?
questions.a: About 20 feet (about 6 meters).

questions.q: What happens in the small intestine?
questions.a: Food is broken down more and nutrients are absorbed into the blood.

days.guide: Explain that fiber (in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, beans) and water help food move smoothly through the intestines. The child names 3 high-fiber foods they like.

questions.q: How do fiber and water help digestion?
questions.a: Fiber adds bulk and water softens waste so it moves easily through the intestines and prevents constipation.

questions.q: Name two high-fiber foods.
questions.a: Any two: apples, berries, beans, broccoli, oatmeal, whole-wheat bread, carrots.

days.guide: The child writes the digestion steps in order with one sentence per organ, using the diagram only if stuck.

questions.q: What does the large intestine do?
questions.a: It absorbs water from leftover food and forms waste.

weeks.assessment_key: Digestion sequence key: 1) Mouth – teeth chew, saliva starts breaking down food; 2) Esophagus – a tube that squeezes food down to the stomach; 3) Stomach – muscles churn food with acid and juices into mush; 4) Small intestine – food is broken down further and nutrients pass into the blood; 5) Large intestine – water is absorbed and waste forms; 6) Waste leaves the body. Proficient: all organs in correct order with a correct job for at least 4.

weeks.prep: Paper towel tube, a plastic bottle (cut the bottom off), 2 balloons, scissors and tape for the lung model (adult cuts). A stopwatch for pulse. Graph paper.
misconceptions: Thinking the heart is on the far left of the chest. It sits near the center, tilted slightly left.
Thinking the lungs are muscles that push air. The diaphragm muscle below the lungs pulls down to draw air in.

days.guide: Explain that the heart is a fist-sized muscle that pumps blood. The child listens to your heartbeat by placing a paper towel tube on your chest (quiet room) and counts beats.

questions.q: What kind of organ is the heart, and what does it do?
questions.a: It is a muscle that pumps blood through the body.

questions.q: About how big is your heart?
questions.a: About the size of your fist.

days.guide: Find the pulse at the wrist or neck, count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Then do 1 minute of jumping jacks and measure again. Graph both.

questions.q: You counted 25 beats in 15 seconds. What is your pulse per minute?
questions.a: 100 beats per minute (25 × 4).

questions.q: Why does your pulse go up when you exercise?
questions.a: Your muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster to deliver it.

days.guide: Build the model: balloon inside the bottle (lung), a balloon stretched across the open bottom (diaphragm). Pull the bottom balloon down and the inner balloon inflates.

questions.q: What happens when you pull the bottom balloon down, and what part of the body is it?
questions.a: The inner balloon fills with air; the bottom balloon is the diaphragm.

questions.q: What gas do your lungs take in that your body needs?
questions.a: Oxygen.

days.guide: Brainstorm with the child how to protect the heart and lungs: exercise, healthy food, no smoking or vaping, avoid secondhand smoke, stay inside on bad air days.

questions.q: Name two ways to keep your heart and lungs healthy.
questions.a: Any two: regular exercise, eat healthy foods, never smoke or vape, avoid secondhand smoke and polluted air.

days.guide: The child explains aloud or in writing how the heart and lungs work together; prompt with 'Where does oxygen go after it enters the lungs?'

questions.q: How do the heart and lungs work together?
questions.a: Lungs bring oxygen into the blood; the heart pumps that blood to the body and brings blood with carbon dioxide back to the lungs to breathe out.

weeks.assessment_key: Heart-lung explanation key: a proficient explanation says the lungs take in oxygen from the air; oxygen passes into the blood; the heart (a muscle) pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body; blood brings carbon dioxide back, and the heart pumps it to the lungs to be breathed out; exercise makes both work faster. Rubric: 4 = all of these ideas in order; 3 = most ideas with one gap; 2 = describes heart and lungs separately without the connection; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: A blindfold, 4–5 small food samples (check allergies), a 12-inch ruler, and a bike helmet. Senses chart template with columns: sense, organ, job, how to protect.
misconceptions: Thinking a helmet only matters on long or fast rides. Most head injuries happen close to home and at low speeds; always wear one.
Thinking taste works alone. Much of flavor comes from smell, which is why food tastes bland with a stuffy nose.

days.guide: Explain the brain is the control center sending messages through nerves. Show how a helmet absorbs impact (optional: egg in a padded cup vs. not). The child lists 4 activities that need a helmet.

questions.q: What is the brain's job?
questions.a: It is the control center: it controls movement, thinking, feelings and the senses by sending and receiving messages through nerves.

questions.q: Name two activities where you should wear a helmet.
questions.a: Biking, scootering, skateboarding, roller skating, skiing, horseback riding.

days.guide: Hold a ruler at the top with the 0 end just above the child's open fingers; drop it without warning and note the cm/inch where they catch it. Repeat 5 times and record.

questions.q: If you caught the ruler at 15 cm, then 12 cm, then 9 cm, what is happening?
questions.a: Your reaction time is getting faster (a smaller number means a quicker catch), likely from practice.

questions.q: What carries the message from your eyes to your hand?
questions.a: Nerves carry signals from the eyes to the brain and from the brain to the hand muscles.

days.guide: Blindfold the child and give small tastes (apple, lemon, salty cracker). Then have them hold their nose and try again; discuss how smell helps taste.

questions.q: Why does food taste different when you hold your nose?
questions.a: Smell is a big part of flavor; without smell, the brain gets less information about the food.

days.guide: List ways to protect eyes (sunglasses, goggles for sports or tools, never look at the sun) and ears (keep headphone volume at or below half, move away from loud sounds).

questions.q: How can you protect your hearing when using headphones?
questions.a: Keep the volume low (about half or less) and take breaks.

questions.q: Why should you never look directly at the sun?
questions.a: It can permanently damage the eyes.

days.guide: The child completes the senses chart for all 5 senses.

questions.q: Which organ is used for touch?
questions.a: The skin.

weeks.assessment_key: Senses chart key: Sight – eyes – see light, color, shape – sunglasses, safety goggles, don't stare at sun; Hearing – ears – hear sounds – keep volume low, earplugs at loud events; Smell – nose – detect odors, warn of smoke/spoiled food – avoid sniffing chemicals; Taste – tongue – sweet, salty, sour, bitter, savory – don't taste unknown things; Touch – skin – feel pressure, heat, pain – gloves, sunscreen. Proficient: all 5 rows with correct organ and job and a reasonable protection.

weeks.prep: Baby photos of the child, a height chart or measuring tape. Preview a check-up description (e.g., KidsHealth 'Going to the Doctor'). Prepare the Unit 2 quiz below.
misconceptions: Thinking being shorter or taller than friends means something is wrong. Kids grow at different rates because of genes, nutrition and sleep; this is normal.
Thinking doctors are only for when you're sick. Check-ups help keep you healthy and catch problems early.

days.guide: Look at baby photos and compare to now. Measure the child's height and mark it on the chart; list things they can do now that they couldn't as a baby.

questions.q: Name two ways your body has changed since you were a baby.
questions.a: Any two: taller, heavier, more teeth (adult teeth coming in), can walk/run, can talk and read.

days.guide: Discuss that friends and siblings grow at different speeds and that genes, food, sleep and activity affect growth.

questions.q: Why do kids the same age grow at different rates?
questions.a: Growth depends on genes from parents, nutrition, sleep and activity; everyone has their own timetable.

questions.q: What can you do to help your body grow healthy?
questions.a: Eat a variety of healthy foods, get 9–12 hours of sleep, and be active.

days.guide: The child lists trusted adults (parents, grandparents, doctor, school nurse) they can ask about body questions.

questions.q: Who could you ask if you have a question about your body?
questions.a: A parent or caregiver, doctor, nurse or another trusted adult.

days.guide: Describe a check-up: height, weight, heart and lungs with a stethoscope, eyes and ears, reflexes, maybe vaccines. Let the child ask questions and list one to ask at their next visit.

questions.q: What does the doctor use to listen to your heart and lungs?
questions.a: A stethoscope.

questions.q: Why do we go to the doctor when we're not sick?
questions.a: For check-ups to make sure we're growing well, get vaccines, and catch any problems early.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 quiz orally or in writing.

questions.q: Which organ is the control center of the body?
questions.a: The brain.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 quiz key: 1) Skull protects the brain. 2) Calcium makes bones hard. 3) Elbow = hinge joint; shoulder = ball-and-socket. 4) Muscles work in pairs because they can only pull. 5) Digestion order: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. 6) Nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. 7) The heart is a muscle that pumps blood. 8) Lungs take in oxygen. 9) Brain = control center. 10) Kids grow at different rates and that is normal. 8–10 correct = proficient.

weeks.prep: A feelings chart (search 'feelings wheel for kids') and a journal. Model your own feelings honestly during the week.
misconceptions: Thinking some feelings are 'bad.' All feelings are normal; what matters is how we express them.
Thinking an I-message blames: 'I feel mad because you're mean.' A real I-message describes the action, not the person: 'I feel mad when you take my pencil without asking because I need it.'

days.guide: Together, list 20 feeling words (happy, proud, nervous, frustrated, lonely, excited, embarrassed, jealous, calm…). The child acts out 5 for you to guess.

questions.q: Give a 'stronger' word for 'mad' and for 'happy.'
questions.a: Mad: furious or angry. Happy: thrilled, joyful or ecstatic.

days.guide: On a body outline, the child colors where they feel anger (hot face, clenched fists), worry (stomach ache, tight chest) and excitement (racing heart, energy).

questions.q: What might your body do when you are angry?
questions.a: Face gets hot, fists clench, heart beats fast, muscles tighten.

questions.q: Why is it useful to notice body signals?
questions.a: They are early warnings that help you recognize a feeling and calm down before acting.

days.guide: Make two columns: healthy and unhealthy ways to express anger. Sort cards (yell at someone, hit a pillow, take deep breaths, slam a door, talk to an adult, draw).

questions.q: Is hitting a person a healthy way to show anger? What could you do instead?
questions.a: No. Instead: take deep breaths, walk away, talk to a trusted adult, use an I-message, or squeeze a stress ball.

days.guide: The child writes a journal entry: 2–3 feelings from today and what caused them.

questions.q: Can you feel two feelings at once? Give an example.
questions.a: Yes, e.g., excited and nervous before a game or a first day.

days.guide: Teach the I-message frame. Role-play: a sibling grabbed your book. The child says a complete I-message calmly.

questions.q: Turn 'You're so annoying!' into an I-message.
questions.a: Example: 'I feel frustrated when you interrupt me because I lose my place.'

weeks.assessment_key: Feelings journal and role-play rubric: 4 = journal uses at least 2 specific feeling words and explains what caused them; the role-play uses a complete I-message ('I feel ___ when ___ because ___') in a calm voice; 3 = journal and I-message with one missing part; 2 = vague words ('good/bad') and incomplete I-message; 1 = not attempted.

weeks.prep: A shoebox, stress ball, paper and crayons, a favorite book and index cards for breathing instructions.
misconceptions: Thinking all stress is bad. A little stress can help you get ready (before a test or game); it's too much stress for too long that needs managing.
Thinking calm-down strategies only work once you're very upset. Practice them when calm so they're ready when needed.

days.guide: Ask what stress feels like (tight muscles, worried thoughts, stomachache). The child lists 5 things that cause them stress.

questions.q: What is stress?
questions.a: The feeling of pressure or worry the body and mind have when facing something hard or new.

questions.q: Name two signs your body is stressed.
questions.a: Any two: fast heartbeat, stomachache, headache, tight muscles, trouble sleeping, sweaty hands.

days.guide: Model belly breathing (hand on belly, breathe in slowly through the nose so the belly rises, out through the mouth). Then 5-finger breathing: trace up a finger breathing in, down breathing out. Practice 3 minutes.

questions.q: How do you do 5-finger breathing?
questions.a: Trace up each finger while breathing in and down while breathing out, for all 5 fingers.

questions.q: Why does slow breathing help you calm down?
questions.a: It slows the heart rate and relaxes the body, telling the brain you're safe.

days.guide: The child decorates a shoebox and fills it: stress ball, paper and crayons, favorite book, breathing cards. Decide together where the kit lives.

questions.q: What would you put in a calm-down kit and why?
questions.a: Items that soothe: a stress ball to squeeze, drawing supplies, a book, breathing cards, a soft item.

days.guide: Try 3 movement relievers for 2 minutes each (stretching, a brisk walk, a dance break). The child rates each 1–5 for how calm they felt.

questions.q: Why can moving your body reduce stress?
questions.a: Exercise uses up stress energy and releases chemicals that improve mood.

days.guide: The child makes a poster with their 4 best strategies in order (first try…, then…). Post it near the calm-down kit.

questions.q: If breathing doesn't help, what's your next step?
questions.a: Answer names the next strategy on their poster, ending with talking to a trusted adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Calm-down plan poster rubric: 4 = lists 4 specific strategies the child tested (e.g., belly breathing, 5-finger breathing, dance break, calm-down kit) in a sensible order and names a trusted adult to go to; 3 = 4 strategies but not ordered or vague; 2 = 2–3 strategies; 1 = fewer than 2.

weeks.prep: Borrow 'The Invisible Boy' by Trudy Ludwig from the library (or another friendship picture book) and read it ahead. Paper for the friendship recipe.
misconceptions: Thinking a friend has to like everything you like. Good friends can be different; respect and kindness matter more than sameness.
Thinking including others is only for adults or teachers to do. Kids can notice someone alone and invite them.

days.guide: The child lists 8 qualities of a good friend and ranks the top 3, explaining why.

questions.q: Name three qualities of a good friend.
questions.a: Any three: kind, honest, loyal, good listener, shares, includes others, helpful, fun, respectful.

days.guide: Read 'The Invisible Boy' aloud. Discuss how Brian felt being left out and what changed when Justin arrived and was kind to him.

questions.q: How did Brian feel at the beginning of the story?
questions.a: Invisible and lonely, because other kids didn't notice or include him.

questions.q: What changed things for Brian?
questions.a: Brian was kind to the new boy, Justin, who then included him; when Brian was invited to work with Justin and another classmate, he began to feel seen.

days.guide: The child interviews a friend or relative and records one thing different about them and one thing they share.

questions.q: What is empathy?
questions.a: Understanding and caring about how someone else feels, like imagining being in their shoes.

days.guide: Brainstorm 3 ways to include someone left out: invite them to play, sit with them, ask their name and what they like.

questions.q: You see a kid alone at the park. What could you say?
questions.a: Example: 'Hi, I'm ___. Want to play with us?'

days.guide: The child writes a 'recipe for friendship' with ingredients and steps.

questions.q: What is one 'ingredient' in your recipe and why?
questions.a: Any friend quality with a reason, e.g., 'honesty, so friends can trust each other.'

weeks.assessment_key: Friendship recipe rubric: 4 = lists at least 5 'ingredients' (qualities such as kindness, honesty, listening, sharing, including others) and 3+ steps that are actions (e.g., 'Mix in listening by asking about their day'); 3 = 3–4 ingredients and 2 steps; 2 = list only, no steps; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Write 6–8 scenario cards of everyday conflicts (shared toy, who goes first, being interrupted, borrowed item broken). Index card for the pocket card.
misconceptions: Thinking conflict resolution means someone wins. The goal is a solution both people can accept.
Trying to solve a conflict while still angry. Step 1 is always to cool down.

days.guide: You tell a short story; the child listens with eyes on you and then repeats the main points and names a feeling you had. Switch roles.

questions.q: What does an active listener do?
questions.a: Looks at the speaker, doesn't interrupt, nods, then repeats back the main points and the feeling.

days.guide: The child writes I-messages for 5 conflicts using 'I feel ___ when ___ because ___.'

questions.q: Write an I-message for when someone cuts in line.
questions.a: Example: 'I feel upset when you cut in front of me because I was waiting my turn.'

days.guide: Teach the 5 steps: cool down, talk (I-message), listen, brainstorm solutions, agree. The child makes a pocket card.

questions.q: What are the 5 conflict-resolution steps in order?
questions.a: Cool down, talk, listen, brainstorm, agree.

questions.q: Why do you cool down first?
questions.a: When you're very angry it's hard to think clearly or listen.

days.guide: Role-play a sibling conflict over a shared toy using the pocket card. Pause to coach each step.

questions.q: Name two fair solutions for two kids who want the same toy.
questions.a: Take turns with a timer, play with it together, or choose a different activity and switch later.

days.guide: The child explains the steps and gives 2 real situations where they could use them.

questions.q: When should you get an adult instead of solving it yourself?
questions.a: When someone is getting hurt, it is bullying, or you've tried the steps and it isn't working.

weeks.assessment_key: Role-play and pocket card rubric: 4 = pocket card lists the 5 steps in order (cool down, talk, listen, brainstorm, agree); in the role-play the child cools down, uses an I-message, listens and repeats back, offers 2+ ideas and agrees on a fair solution; 3 = all steps but one weak; 2 = skips cooling down or listening; 1 = argues without the steps.

weeks.prep: Read the KidsHealth (kidshealth.org/kids) article on bullying ahead of time. Write scenario cards: 2 physical, 2 verbal, 2 social, 2 cyberbullying, plus 2 ordinary conflicts. Parent note: ask gently whether the child has seen or experienced bullying, and follow up if so.
misconceptions: Calling every disagreement bullying. Bullying is repeated, on purpose, and involves a power imbalance; a one-time argument between equals is conflict.
Thinking telling an adult is 'tattling.' Tattling is to get someone in trouble; reporting is to keep someone safe.

days.guide: Read the KidsHealth article together. Make a T-chart: bullying (repeated, on purpose, power imbalance) vs. conflict (disagreement between equals).

questions.q: What three things make something bullying?
questions.a: It is on purpose, it happens repeatedly, and there is a power imbalance (one person has more power).

questions.q: Two friends argue once about a game rule. Is that bullying?
questions.a: No, that's a conflict between equals, not repeated or a power imbalance.

days.guide: The child sorts scenario cards into physical, verbal, social and cyberbullying.

questions.q: Spreading rumors and leaving someone out on purpose is what type of bullying?
questions.a: Social (relational) bullying.

questions.q: Sending mean messages in a game chat over and over is what type?
questions.a: Cyberbullying.

days.guide: Practice the 4 upstander moves with role-play: speak up ('Stop, that's not okay'), stay with the target, walk away together, get help.

questions.q: What is the difference between a bystander and an upstander?
questions.a: A bystander sees bullying and does nothing; an upstander takes safe action to help.

questions.q: Name a safe upstander action that doesn't involve confronting the bully.
questions.a: Walk away with the target, be kind to them later, or tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: The child practices reporting to you: who, what, where, when.

questions.q: What's the difference between tattling and reporting?
questions.a: Tattling tries to get someone in trouble; reporting is to help someone who is hurt or in danger.

days.guide: The child writes and signs an upstander pledge and posts it.

questions.q: What will you do if you see someone bullied online?
questions.a: Don't join in or share it, save or screenshot it, and tell a trusted adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Upstander pledge rubric: 4 = pledge names at least 3 specific actions (speak up, stay with the target, walk away together, get help from an adult, include the target later), is in the child's own words and signed; 3 = 2 actions; 2 = general 'I'll be nice'; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Goal worksheet and a 2-week calendar. Prepare the Unit 3 quiz below.
misconceptions: Thinking people are either smart or not. Brains grow with practice and effort; mistakes help you learn.
Setting a goal without steps. Big goals need small steps and support.

days.guide: Read 6 fixed-mindset statements; the child rewrites each as growth mindset.

questions.q: Change 'I'm bad at math' into a growth-mindset statement.
questions.a: Example: 'Math is hard for me right now, but I'm getting better with practice.'

questions.q: Why does the word 'yet' matter?
questions.a: It shows you can't do it now but can learn with effort.

days.guide: The child chooses a personal goal that matters to them and writes it down.

questions.q: What makes a good personal goal?
questions.a: It is specific, something you care about, and possible to reach with effort.

days.guide: List 4 small steps and names of supporters for each.

questions.q: Goal: read a chapter book. Give a first step.
questions.a: Example: pick a book at the library and read 1 chapter each night.

days.guide: Set up the 2-week calendar; the child checks off each day and notes any obstacle.

questions.q: What should you do when you hit an obstacle?
questions.a: Figure out what went wrong, try a new strategy, ask for help, and keep going.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 quiz.

questions.q: What's one sign of a good friend?
questions.a: Kind, honest, listens, includes you, respects you.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 quiz key: 1) All feelings are normal. 2) I-message frame: I feel ___ when ___ because ___. 3) Two calming strategies: belly breathing, 5-finger breathing, movement, calm-down kit. 4) Two friend qualities (kind, honest, listens, includes). 5) Conflict steps: cool down, talk, listen, brainstorm, agree. 6) Bullying = repeated, on purpose, power imbalance. 7) Four types: physical, verbal, social, cyber. 8) Upstander action: speak up, stay with, walk away together, get help. 9) Reporting is to keep someone safe. 10) Growth mindset example: 'I can't do it yet.' Goal worksheet proficient = clear goal, 4 steps, named supporters. 8–10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Graph paper and pencils; know where your smoke alarms are and how to test them; choose an outside meeting place (a mailbox or a tree). Parent note: keep the tone calm; focus on 'we have a plan.'
misconceptions: Hiding from fire under a bed or in a closet. Get out and stay out; firefighters can't find you if you hide.
Going back inside for pets or toys. Never go back in; tell firefighters who or what is still inside.
Standing up and running through smoke. Smoke rises; crawl low where the air is cleaner.

days.guide: Teach rules: matches and lighters are tools for adults only; tell an adult if you find one; keep 3 feet away from stoves and space heaters. Child finds hazards in a home picture.

questions.q: What should you do if you find matches or a lighter?
questions.a: Don't touch them; tell an adult right away.

questions.q: How far should you stay from space heaters and stoves?
questions.a: At least 3 feet (a 'kid-free zone').

days.guide: Push the test button on each smoke alarm with the child so they know the sound. Explain it means 'get out now.'

questions.q: What should you do when you hear the smoke alarm?
questions.a: Get out of the house right away and go to the meeting place.

questions.q: How often should smoke alarms be tested?
questions.a: Once a month.

days.guide: The child draws the home's floor plan, marks two exits from each room and the meeting place.

questions.q: Why do you need two ways out of every room?
questions.a: In case fire or smoke blocks one exit.

questions.q: Where do you go once you are outside?
questions.a: To the family meeting place, and stay there.

days.guide: Run a drill: sound the alarm, child crawls low, feels a door with the back of the hand, exits and goes to the meeting place. Time it.

questions.q: Why crawl low in smoke?
questions.a: Smoke and heat rise, so cleaner, cooler air is near the floor.

questions.q: What should you do if a door is hot?
questions.a: Don't open it; use your second way out.

days.guide: The child demonstrates stop, drop and roll and explains the escape plan.

questions.q: If your clothes catch fire, what do you do?
questions.a: Stop, drop to the ground, cover your face, and roll until the fire is out.

weeks.assessment_key: Escape plan and drill key: floor plan shows every room with two exits (door and window), arrows to exits, and a marked outside meeting place; the drill is completed with the child crawling low, feeling doors with the back of the hand before opening, and going straight to the meeting place (aim: out in under 2 minutes). Stop, drop and roll: stop where you are, drop to the ground, cover your face with your hands, roll back and forth until the flames are out. Proficient: all parts correct.

weeks.prep: Bike helmet (check it fits and isn't cracked), bicycle, a planned short walking route with a crosswalk. Know California law: children under 8 ride in a car seat or booster in the back seat; children under 8 who are 4'9" or taller may use a seat belt; kids under 13 should ride in the back seat. Bike helmets are required by law for riders under 18 in California.
misconceptions: Thinking the green walk light means it's always safe to go. Still look left-right-left and watch for turning cars.
Wearing the helmet tipped back on the forehead. It should sit level, about 2 fingers above the eyebrows.

days.guide: Walk a route with a crosswalk. At each corner the child stops at the curb, looks left-right-left, listens, and crosses only when clear.

questions.q: What do you do before crossing a street?
questions.a: Stop at the curb, look left, right and left again, listen for cars, and cross when it's clear, preferably at a crosswalk.

questions.q: If there is no sidewalk, which way do you walk?
questions.a: Facing traffic, on the left side, as far from the road as possible.

days.guide: Fit the helmet: Eyes — look up and see the rim (2 fingers above brows); Ears — straps make a V under each ear; Mouth — open wide and the helmet hugs the head; buckle snug with only 1–2 fingers under the strap.

questions.q: What is the eyes-ears-mouth test?
questions.a: Eyes: you can see the helmet rim when looking up (about 2 fingers above eyebrows). Ears: straps form a V just under the ears. Mouth: opening wide makes the helmet hug your head.

days.guide: Teach hand signals (left turn: left arm straight out; right turn: right arm straight out or left arm bent up; stop: left arm bent down). Ride a short safe route signaling turns.

questions.q: Show the hand signal for stopping.
questions.a: Left arm bent down at the elbow, palm facing back.

questions.q: Which side of the road do bikes ride on?
questions.a: The right side, in the same direction as traffic.

days.guide: Explain booster seat rules and do the 5-step seat belt test in the car.

questions.q: What are the 5 steps of the seat-belt fit test?
questions.a: Back against the seat; knees bend at the seat edge; lap belt low on the upper thighs/hips; shoulder belt across the middle of the chest and shoulder (not the neck); can stay seated like that the whole trip.

questions.q: Where should kids under 13 sit in the car?
questions.a: In the back seat.

days.guide: The child completes the checklist and explains each item.

questions.q: Why wear bright clothes when walking or biking?
questions.a: So drivers can see you, especially at dusk or in bad weather.

weeks.assessment_key: Safety checklist key: Pedestrian – stop at the curb, look left-right-left, listen, cross at crosswalks, walk facing traffic if no sidewalk, make eye contact with drivers. Bike – helmet fits (eyes-ears-mouth), ride on the right with traffic, use hand signals, obey stop signs, bright clothing. Passenger – booster seat until the seat belt fits (usually 4'9"), back seat under 13, buckle every ride, 5-step test passes. Proficient: child can explain each item.

weeks.prep: A properly sized U.S. Coast Guard-approved life jacket. Preview a rip current graphic (weather.gov/safety/ripcurrent). Write 4 outdoor scenario cards.
misconceptions: Swimming straight back to shore in a rip current. Swim parallel to the shore until out of the current, or float and signal for help.
Jumping in to save a struggling swimmer. 'Reach or throw, don't go': extend a pole or throw something that floats and call for an adult.
Thinking pool toys or water wings replace life jackets. Only a Coast Guard-approved life jacket is a safety device.

days.guide: Teach pool, lake and ocean rules. Show the rip current graphic and practice the escape motion (swim sideways/parallel).

questions.q: What is a rip current, and how do you escape one?
questions.a: A strong, narrow current flowing away from shore. Don't fight it; swim parallel to the shore until free, then swim in, or float and wave for help.

questions.q: Who should always be watching when you swim?
questions.a: An adult who knows how to swim (and a lifeguard at beaches and public pools).

days.guide: The child puts on the life jacket. Check: label shows it is Coast Guard-approved and fits the child's weight; all buckles fastened; lift at the shoulders — it shouldn't ride above the chin or ears.

questions.q: How do you check if a life jacket fits?
questions.a: Buckle it, then have an adult lift it at the shoulders; it should not slide up past the chin or ears.

days.guide: Explain the buddy system. Practice 'reach or throw, don't go' with a towel or pool noodle.

questions.q: If your friend is struggling in the water, what should you do?
questions.a: Don't jump in. Reach with a pole or towel or throw something that floats, and shout for an adult.

questions.q: What is the buddy system?
questions.a: Always swimming with a partner who keeps track of you and can get help.

days.guide: Use decide-act-check on 4 scenarios: thunder at the beach (get out of the water and go indoors); lost on a hike (stop, stay put, hug a tree, blow a whistle); etc.

questions.q: What should you do if you hear thunder at the beach?
questions.a: Get out of the water and go inside a building or hard-topped car; 'when thunder roars, go indoors.'

questions.q: What should you do if you get lost on a hike?
questions.a: Stop and stay where you are, stay calm, blow a whistle or call out, and wait for help.

days.guide: The child makes a water safety poster with 5 rules and pictures.

questions.q: Name one rule for diving.
questions.a: Never dive into shallow or unknown water; go in feet first.

weeks.assessment_key: Water safety poster key (any 5 correct rules): swim only with an adult watching; always swim with a buddy; wear a life jacket on boats and in open water; swim parallel to shore to escape a rip current; reach or throw, don't go; get out of the water when you hear thunder; feet first into water you don't know; swim near a lifeguard. Rubric: 4 = 5 accurate rules with pictures; 3 = 4; 2 = 2–3; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: A toy or unplugged phone, the home first aid kit (bandages, gauze, antiseptic wipes, gloves). Make sure the child knows the full home address. Know: for a nosebleed, sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes.
misconceptions: Tilting the head back for a nosebleed. Lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose so blood doesn't run down the throat.
Thinking 911 is for any problem. 911 is for emergencies when someone is hurt, in danger, or there's a fire or crime; for small problems, tell an adult.
Hanging up on 911 first. Stay on the line until the dispatcher says to hang up.

days.guide: The child sorts 12 situations: emergencies (fire, someone not breathing, car crash, someone badly bleeding) vs. non-emergencies (scraped knee, lost toy, power out).

questions.q: Is a scraped knee a 911 emergency?
questions.a: No. Tell an adult and clean and bandage it.

questions.q: Name two situations where you should call 911.
questions.a: Any two: fire, someone unconscious or not breathing, serious injury or bleeding, a crime or someone breaking in, a car crash.

days.guide: Practice a pretend 911 call: stay calm, say your name, full address, what happened, answer questions, and don't hang up.

questions.q: What three things should you tell the 911 dispatcher first?
questions.a: Your name, your address (where you are), and what happened.

questions.q: When can you hang up?
questions.a: Only when the dispatcher tells you to.

days.guide: Show how to clean a small cut (wash with soap and water, press with gauze if bleeding, bandage). Practice nosebleed care. Tour the first aid kit.

questions.q: What do you do for a nosebleed?
questions.a: Sit up, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose for about 10 minutes.

questions.q: How do you care for a small scrape?
questions.a: Wash it with soap and water, gently pat dry, and cover with a bandage; tell an adult.

days.guide: Practice drop, cover and hold on in 3 rooms; find safe spots (under a sturdy table, away from windows and tall furniture).

questions.q: What are the three steps during an earthquake?
questions.a: Drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck (under a sturdy table if you can), and hold on until the shaking stops.

questions.q: Where is NOT a safe spot in an earthquake?
questions.a: Near windows, under heavy things that could fall, or in a doorway (modern advice is to get under a table).

days.guide: The child makes and laminates (or tapes) an emergency contact card.

questions.q: What is the number for Poison Control?

weeks.assessment_key: Emergency contact card key: child's full name, full home address with city and ZIP, parent/caregiver names and cell numbers, one trusted neighbor or relative with phone number, '911 for emergencies,' and Poison Control 1-800-222-1222. Proficient: all items present and the child can read/say them without help.

weeks.prep: Write 10 scenario cards (e.g., a neighbor you know offers a ride without asking your parent; a stranger asks for help finding a puppy; a friend's parent invites you over). Parent note: preview the body-safety lesson (Day 4); use correct names for body parts and keep the tone matter-of-fact. Reassure the child they will never be in trouble for telling you.
misconceptions: Thinking only strangers can be unsafe. Most rules are about situations: any adult who asks you to keep a secret, go somewhere without checking, or touches you in a way that feels wrong is breaking the rules.
Thinking surprises and secrets are the same. Surprises (like a gift) end with everyone happy soon; secrets that make you uncomfortable should always be told to a trusted adult.

days.guide: The child sorts scenario cards into safe, unsafe or check with an adult.

questions.q: An adult you don't know asks you to help find a lost puppy. Safe or unsafe?
questions.a: Unsafe. Adults should ask other adults for help; say no, get away and tell a trusted adult.

questions.q: A friend's parent invites you over. What should you do?
questions.a: Check with your parent or caregiver first.

days.guide: Trace the child's hand; on each finger they write a trusted adult they could tell anything to.

questions.q: What makes someone a trusted adult?
questions.a: An adult who keeps you safe, listens and helps, like a parent, grandparent, teacher or doctor.

days.guide: Teach 'say no, get away, tell someone.' Practice a loud firm 'NO!' with feet planted and eye contact.

questions.q: What are the three refusal steps for unsafe situations?
questions.a: Say no, get away, tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Teach body safety calmly: your body belongs to you; private parts are the parts covered by a swimsuit; no one should touch them or ask you to touch theirs except for health reasons with a parent present; never keep secrets about touching.

questions.q: If someone asks you to keep a secret about touching, what should you do?
questions.a: Never keep it; tell a trusted adult right away. You will not be in trouble.

questions.q: What is the difference between a surprise and a secret?
questions.a: A surprise is fun and will be told soon (like a birthday gift); an unsafe secret makes you feel bad and should be told.

days.guide: Role-play 3 refusal scenarios with you playing the other person.

questions.q: Show how you would say no with your body.
questions.a: Stand tall, feet planted, look the person in the eye, and say 'No!' in a loud, firm voice.

weeks.assessment_key: Refusal role-play rubric: across 3 scenarios the child 4 = says 'No' clearly with a firm voice, eye contact and strong posture, gets away, and names who they would tell; 3 = does all three steps but with a weak voice or hesitation; 2 = says no but doesn't leave or tell; 1 = goes along with the scenario.

weeks.prep: A computer or tablet. Look up guidance on passphrases. Prepare the family technology agreement template and the Unit 4 quiz below.
misconceptions: Thinking people online are who they say they are. Anyone can pretend to be a kid online.
Thinking it's fine to share a password with a best friend. Passwords are shared only with parents.

days.guide: Sort info cards into okay to share online (favorite color, pet's type) and private (full name, address, school, phone, photos, birthday, passwords).

questions.q: Is it okay to post your school name online?
questions.a: No. It's private because it tells strangers where to find you.

questions.q: Name two things that are private online.
questions.a: Any two: full name, address, phone number, school, passwords, photos of yourself, birthday.

days.guide: Create a passphrase of 3–4 random words with a number or symbol. Explain only parents get to know it.

questions.q: Who should you share your password with?
questions.a: Only your parents or guardians.

questions.q: Which is stronger: 'max123' or 'purple-taco-river-7'?
questions.a: 'purple-taco-river-7', because it is longer and harder to guess.

days.guide: Discuss: if someone online asks personal questions, wants photos, asks to keep a secret or to meet, stop, don't reply, and tell a parent.

questions.q: Someone in a game asks where you live. What do you do?
questions.a: Don't answer, stop chatting, and tell a parent.

questions.q: Is it ever okay to meet an online friend in person alone?
questions.a: No. Never; always tell a parent.

days.guide: Write a family tech agreement together: times, allowed apps, where devices are used, what to do if something online is upsetting. Everyone signs.

questions.q: What should you do if you see something online that makes you uncomfortable?
questions.a: Close it or turn off the screen and tell a parent.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 quiz.

questions.q: What should you do if you hear the smoke alarm?
questions.a: Get out right away and go to the meeting place.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 quiz key: 1) Get out and stay out in a fire; crawl low under smoke. 2) Stop, drop and roll. 3) Test smoke alarms monthly. 4) Look left-right-left before crossing. 5) Helmet: eyes-ears-mouth test. 6) Escape a rip current by swimming parallel to shore. 7) Reach or throw, don't go. 8) Tell the 911 dispatcher your name, address and what happened. 9) Earthquake: drop, cover, hold on. 10) Never share your address, school or password online. Tech agreement proficient: includes screen time limits, allowed apps, what to do if something online feels wrong, and is signed. 8–10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Empty medicine boxes (pain reliever, cough medicine, vitamins); remove any pills. Store real medicine out of reach. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222.
misconceptions: Thinking more medicine works faster or better. Taking more than the label says can be dangerous.
Thinking medicine prescribed for someone else is safe for you. Prescriptions are made for one person's body and illness only.
Thinking vitamins are candy. They're medicine-like and can make you sick in large amounts.

days.guide: Define: a drug is any substance that changes how the body or mind works; a medicine is a drug used to prevent or treat illness. Sort examples (cough syrup, caffeine, nicotine, antibiotics, alcohol).

questions.q: What is the difference between a medicine and a drug?
questions.a: All medicines are drugs, but a medicine is used to prevent or treat illness; some drugs (like nicotine and alcohol) are harmful and not medicine.

questions.q: Is nicotine a medicine?
questions.a: No, it is a harmful, addictive drug.

days.guide: Read a medicine box together: find the dose, the age or weight it's for, how often, and warnings.

questions.q: Why does a medicine label list ages?
questions.a: Doses are different for different ages and sizes; the wrong amount can be harmful.

questions.q: What is the difference between over-the-counter and prescription medicine?
questions.a: Over-the-counter can be bought without a doctor's order; prescription medicine requires a doctor's order and is for one specific person.

days.guide: Teach the rule: only take medicine from a parent or trusted adult, never alone.

questions.q: You find a pill on the floor. What do you do?
questions.a: Don't touch or take it; tell an adult.

questions.q: Your friend offers you some of her allergy medicine. What should you say?
questions.a: No thanks. Only take medicine from your own parent or trusted adult.

days.guide: Show pictures of medicine and candy that look alike. Ask the child to guess which is which and discuss why that's dangerous.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous that some medicines look like candy?
questions.a: Young children might eat them thinking they are candy and could get very sick.

questions.q: What number do you call if someone swallows medicine by accident?
questions.a: Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if they are not breathing or unconscious.

days.guide: The child writes 5 rules for a younger child, in simple words with pictures.

questions.q: What is the most important medicine rule?
questions.a: Only take medicine given by a parent or trusted adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Medicine safety rules key (5 rules for a younger child, any 5 accurate): 1) Only take medicine from a parent or trusted adult. 2) Never take someone else's medicine. 3) Medicine is not candy. 4) Follow the label or doctor's directions exactly. 5) Never take medicine you find. 6) Tell an adult if you feel sick after taking medicine. Rubric: 4 = 5 accurate rules in kid-friendly words; 3 = 4; 2 = 2–3; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: Read the KidsHealth article on vaping (kidshealth.org) ahead. Find a healthy vs. smoker's lung image (CDC or American Lung Association). Parent note: the images can be upsetting; preview and keep the tone factual.
misconceptions: Thinking vapes are just harmless water vapor. Vape aerosol contains nicotine and other chemicals and tiny particles that harm the lungs.
Thinking you can try it once without problems. Nicotine is highly addictive, especially for young brains.
Thinking secondhand smoke only matters indoors for a long time. Any secondhand smoke is harmful; there's no safe level.

days.guide: Compare the healthy and smoker's lung images. The child lists effects on the lungs (damage, coughing, cancer, trouble breathing) and heart (faster heartbeat, heart disease).

questions.q: Name two effects of smoking on the body.
questions.a: Any two: lung damage, lung cancer, heart disease, coughing, shortness of breath, stained teeth, bad breath.

questions.q: What is the addictive drug in tobacco?
questions.a: Nicotine.

days.guide: Read the vaping article. The child highlights 3 facts.

questions.q: Is vape 'smoke' just water vapor?
questions.a: No. It's an aerosol with nicotine, flavoring chemicals and tiny particles that can harm the lungs.

questions.q: Why is nicotine especially harmful for kids?
questions.a: Their brains are still developing, so they can get addicted more easily, and it can affect attention and learning.

days.guide: Discuss secondhand smoke and how to avoid it (move away, ask to open a window, ask adults not to smoke in the car).

questions.q: What is secondhand smoke?
questions.a: Smoke breathed in by people near someone smoking.

questions.q: How can you avoid secondhand smoke?
questions.a: Move away from smokers, go to a smoke-free area, and ask adults politely not to smoke around you or in the car.

days.guide: Look at how vapes are marketed: candy flavors, bright packaging, social media, friends. Discuss why companies do this.

questions.q: Why do vapes come in candy or fruit flavors?
questions.a: To make them appealing to young people and hide the harsh taste, which is a trick to get new users.

days.guide: The child writes 5 facts about tobacco and vaping.

questions.q: What is the legal age to buy tobacco or vapes in California?

weeks.assessment_key: Tobacco facts key (any 5 accurate): cigarettes and vapes contain nicotine, which is addictive; smoking damages lungs and causes lung cancer and heart disease; smoking makes the heart beat faster and narrows blood vessels; vape aerosol is not just water vapor and contains harmful chemicals; secondhand smoke harms people nearby; the legal age to buy tobacco and vapes is 21; smoking stains teeth and causes bad breath and less stamina. Rubric: 4 = 5 accurate facts; 3 = 4; 2 = 2–3; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: A simple brain diagram (cerebrum, cerebellum, brain stem). Clear space and an adult spotter for the spinning activity (soft surface, stop if the child feels sick). Parent note: if alcohol use is part of family life, explain that adults can choose to drink responsibly but it is harmful to kids.
misconceptions: Thinking alcohol is a stimulant that makes people more active. Alcohol is a depressant; it slows the brain and body.
Thinking a little alcohol is fine for kids. Growing brains are especially sensitive; it's illegal and harmful under 21.

days.guide: Explain that alcohol is a depressant drug that slows messages in the brain, affecting judgment, balance, speech and reaction time. Point to brain areas.

questions.q: Does alcohol speed up or slow down the brain?
questions.a: It slows it down; alcohol is a depressant.

questions.q: Name two things alcohol affects.
questions.a: Judgment, balance, coordination, speech, memory, reaction time.

days.guide: With an adult spotter, the child spins slowly 5 times then tries to walk a straight line. Discuss how alcohol similarly affects balance.

questions.q: Why was it hard to walk the line?
questions.a: Spinning confused the balance system; alcohol also impairs balance and coordination.

days.guide: Explain the brain keeps developing until the mid-20s and alcohol can harm it. The legal age is 21 to protect young people.

questions.q: Why is alcohol especially harmful for kids?
questions.a: Their brains and bodies are still growing, and alcohol can damage development and affect learning and memory.

questions.q: What is the legal drinking age in the U.S.?

days.guide: Look at ads or TV scenes showing alcohol. Discuss what message they send (fun, friends, relaxing) and what they leave out.

questions.q: What do alcohol ads usually leave out?
questions.a: The harmful effects: accidents, poor decisions, illness and addiction.

days.guide: Give the 6-question alcohol quiz.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous to drink and drive?
questions.a: Alcohol slows reaction time and impairs judgment and coordination, causing crashes.

weeks.assessment_key: Alcohol quiz key: 1) Alcohol is a depressant; it slows the brain. 2) It harms judgment (decision making). 3) It harms balance and coordination. 4) It slows reaction time, which is why drinking and driving is dangerous. 5) The legal age to buy or drink alcohol in the U.S. is 21. 6) It is especially harmful to kids because their brains are still growing. Proficient: 5–6 correct.

weeks.prep: Scenario cards about being offered a vape or alcohol; poster board and markers. Prepare the Unit 5 quiz below.
misconceptions: Thinking peer pressure is always bad. Positive peer pressure (friends encouraging you to try out for a team or study) can help.
Thinking you need a long excuse to refuse. A firm 'No thanks' is enough.

days.guide: Define peer pressure (influence from people your age). List positive examples and negative ones.

questions.q: Give an example of positive peer pressure.
questions.a: A friend encouraging you to join a team, study, try a new healthy food, or be kind to someone.

days.guide: Teach the 5 ways to say no; model each with a different voice and body language.

questions.q: Name the 5 refusal strategies.
questions.a: Say no firmly, give a reason, change the subject, walk away, suggest something else.

days.guide: Role-play 3 scenarios where an older kid offers a vape or alcohol. Coach a firm voice and leaving.

questions.q: An older kid offers you a vape and says 'Everyone does it.' What could you say?
questions.a: Example: 'No thanks, I don't want to get addicted. Let's go shoot hoops instead.' Then walk away and tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: The child designs a drug-free poster with a positive message.

questions.q: Why use a positive message on a poster?
questions.a: Positive messages show the benefits of healthy choices and are more inspiring than scare tactics.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 quiz.

questions.q: What is the addictive drug in vapes?
questions.a: Nicotine.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 quiz key: 1) A medicine treats or prevents illness; take only from a trusted adult. 2) Never take someone else's prescription. 3) Poison Control 1-800-222-1222. 4) Nicotine is the addictive drug in tobacco and vapes. 5) Vape aerosol is not harmless water vapor. 6) Secondhand smoke harms people nearby. 7) Alcohol is a depressant that slows the brain. 8) Legal age for alcohol and tobacco: 21. 9) Five refusal strategies: say no firmly, give a reason, change the subject, walk away, suggest something else. 10) Peer pressure can be positive or negative. Poster proficient: clear positive message, accurate fact, eye-catching. 8–10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Glitter, lotion, soap, a spray bottle of water, large paper. Know the CDC 5 steps: wet, lather, scrub (at least 20 seconds), rinse, dry.
misconceptions: Thinking a quick rinse with water kills germs. Soap and 20 seconds of scrubbing are needed to remove germs.
Thinking antibiotics cure colds. Colds are viruses; antibiotics only work on bacteria.

days.guide: Explain that germs are tiny living things. Bacteria are single-celled living things (some helpful, some cause strep throat); viruses are much smaller and cause colds and flu. Germs spread by touch, droplets, food and water.

questions.q: What is the difference between bacteria and viruses?
questions.a: Bacteria are tiny one-celled organisms (some helpful, some cause illness like strep throat); viruses are much smaller and can only multiply inside living cells (they cause colds and flu).

questions.q: Name two ways germs spread.
questions.a: Touching hands or surfaces, coughs and sneezes, contaminated food or water.

days.guide: Put lotion and glitter on the child's hands, then shake hands with family members and touch a doorknob. Count how many people and objects have glitter.

questions.q: What did the glitter show?
questions.a: How easily germs spread from hands to other people and objects.

days.guide: Wash with the 5 steps for 20 seconds (hum 'Happy Birthday' twice). Then try with glitter: water only vs. soap and scrub.

questions.q: What are the 5 handwashing steps?
questions.a: Wet, lather, scrub for 20 seconds, rinse, dry.

questions.q: Name three times you should wash your hands.
questions.a: Before eating, after the bathroom, after coughing/sneezing, after touching animals, after being outside.

days.guide: Spray water at paper from a few feet to show droplet spread. Practice coughing or sneezing into the elbow.

questions.q: Why sneeze into your elbow rather than your hand?
questions.a: So germs don't get on your hands and then spread to things and people you touch.

days.guide: The child makes a handwashing sign for the bathroom.

questions.q: How long should you scrub?
questions.a: At least 20 seconds.
