weeks.assessment_key: Handwashing sign key: the 5 CDC steps in order — 1) Wet hands with clean running water; 2) Lather with soap (backs, between fingers, under nails); 3) Scrub for at least 20 seconds (hum 'Happy Birthday' twice); 4) Rinse; 5) Dry with a clean towel or air dry. Rubric: 4 = all 5 steps in order, 20 seconds mentioned, pictures; 3 = 4 steps; 2 = steps out of order; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Toothbrush, floss, a hand mirror, two hard-boiled eggs (white shells), dark soda, water, two cups. Set up the egg experiment on Day 2 and check on Day 3. Find a Mouth Healthy Kids brushing video (mouthhealthykids.org, American Dental Association).
misconceptions: Thinking baby teeth don't matter because they fall out. They hold space for adult teeth and cavities in them can hurt and cause infections.
Brushing hard and fast. Use gentle small circles for 2 minutes.

days.guide: Use a mirror to find incisors (front, cutting), canines (pointed, tearing), premolars and molars (back, grinding). Name the parts: enamel (hard outer layer), dentin, pulp, root, gums.

questions.q: What do molars do?
questions.a: Grind and crush food.

questions.q: What is the hardest outer layer of a tooth called?
questions.a: Enamel.

days.guide: Place one egg in soda and one in water overnight. The child writes a prediction.

questions.q: Why use an egg?
questions.a: The shell is made of calcium like tooth enamel, so it models how drinks affect teeth.

days.guide: Remove the eggs and compare. Watch the brushing video, then brush for 2 minutes with a timer: small gentle circles, all surfaces, tongue too.

questions.q: What happened to the egg in soda and why?
questions.a: It got stained (and may be softer) because the soda's color and acid affect the calcium shell, like teeth.

questions.q: How long and how often should you brush?
questions.a: 2 minutes, twice a day, with fluoride toothpaste.

days.guide: Model flossing: about 18 inches of floss, wrap on middle fingers, slide gently between teeth and curve in a C shape around each tooth.

questions.q: Why floss?
questions.a: It removes food and plaque between teeth where the toothbrush can't reach.

questions.q: How often should you floss?
questions.a: Once a day.

days.guide: Start the 2-week brushing and flossing tracker and post it in the bathroom.

questions.q: Name two foods or drinks that are bad for teeth and one that's good.
questions.a: Bad: soda, candy, sticky sweets, juice. Good: water, milk, cheese, crunchy vegetables.

weeks.assessment_key: Egg experiment notes key: the egg in soda is stained brown and may feel rougher; the egg in water is unchanged. Conclusion: soda's color and acid can stain and weaken enamel, like teeth. Brushing tracker: proficient = brushing twice a day for 2 minutes and flossing once a day recorded for 14 days, with at least 12 days complete.

weeks.prep: Sleep log, sunscreen (SPF 30+), UV beads or dark construction paper. Know: AASM recommends 9–12 hours of sleep for ages 6–12.
misconceptions: Thinking sunscreen is only needed at the beach or on hot days. UV rays reach you on cloudy days and in winter.
Thinking sleep is wasted time. During sleep the brain stores memories and the body grows and repairs.

days.guide: Explain sleep needs (9–12 hours) and why: memory, growth, mood, fighting germs. The child lists 3 good bedtime habits.

questions.q: How many hours of sleep do kids your age need?
questions.a: 9 to 12 hours.

questions.q: Name two good bedtime habits.
questions.a: No screens an hour before bed, same bedtime every night, a quiet dark room, reading, a calm routine.

days.guide: The child records bedtime and wake time each night and calculates hours slept.

questions.q: You went to bed at 8:30 p.m. and woke at 6:30 a.m. How long did you sleep?
questions.a: 10 hours.

days.guide: Teach sun safety: SPF 30+ sunscreen, reapply every 2 hours, hats, shade from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Test sunscreen on UV beads (or cover half of dark paper with a sunscreen-coated plastic bag) in sunlight.

questions.q: What did sunscreen do to the UV beads (or paper)?
questions.a: The beads under sunscreen changed color less, showing sunscreen blocks UV rays.

questions.q: When is the sun strongest?
questions.a: About 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

days.guide: The child creates a morning and evening hygiene checklist.

questions.q: Why is daily bathing and wearing clean clothes important?
questions.a: It removes sweat, dirt and germs, prevents odor and skin problems, and helps you feel good.

days.guide: Analyze the 5-night log: find the average and set a bedtime goal.

questions.q: If you slept 9, 10, 8, 10 and 8 hours, what's the average?

weeks.assessment_key: Sleep log analysis and hygiene checklist key: analysis correctly computes hours slept each night (e.g., bedtime 9:00 p.m., wake 7:00 a.m. = 10 hours), finds the average, compares to 9–12 hours and sets a specific bedtime goal. Hygiene checklist proficient: morning (brush teeth, wash face, deodorant if needed, brush hair, clean clothes) and evening (bathe/shower, brush and floss, trim/clean nails weekly, lay out clean clothes). Rubric: 4 = all correct and complete; 3 = one math error or missing item; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Arrange a short phone or in-person interview with a health worker (relative who is a nurse, family dentist, etc.). Plan a pharmacy visit at a quiet time. Interview questions sheet.
misconceptions: Thinking pharmacists just hand out boxes. They check that medicines are safe together and the dose is right, and answer questions.
Thinking public health is only hospitals. Public health workers inspect restaurants, test water and track diseases.

days.guide: The child lists 6 health helpers and their jobs.

questions.q: What does an optometrist do?
questions.a: Examines eyes, checks vision, and prescribes glasses or contacts.

questions.q: What does a pharmacist do?
questions.a: Prepares and gives out medicines, checks that they are safe, and explains how to use them.

days.guide: The child interviews a health worker with 5 prepared questions and takes notes.

questions.q: Write one good interview question.
questions.a: Examples: 'What does a typical day look like?' 'What training did you need?' 'How do you help keep people healthy?'

days.guide: At the pharmacy counter, the child observes and asks (if appropriate) how pharmacists keep medicine safe.

questions.q: Name one way a pharmacist keeps medicine safe.
questions.a: Checks the dose, checks for harmful interactions with other medicines, labels clearly, and explains how to take it.

days.guide: Explain public health: inspectors check restaurant kitchens, water treatment plants clean water, and health departments track outbreaks and give vaccines.

questions.q: How do public health workers keep restaurants safe?
questions.a: They inspect kitchens to make sure food is stored, cooked and handled safely and the place is clean.

days.guide: The child completes the booklet.

questions.q: Who would you see for a toothache?
questions.a: A dentist.

weeks.assessment_key: Health helpers booklet rubric: 4 = at least 6 pages (doctor – checks health and treats illness; nurse – cares for patients, gives shots; dentist – cares for teeth; pharmacist – fills prescriptions and explains medicine; school nurse – first aid and health at school; optometrist – checks eyes and prescribes glasses) each with an accurate job and picture, plus the interview page; 3 = 4–5 pages accurate; 2 = 2–3 pages or errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: AirNow website (airnow.gov) bookmarked. Gloves, a bathroom scale or kitchen scale, 3 bins for trash audit. Know AQI levels: 0–50 green/good, 51–100 yellow/moderate, 101–150 orange/unhealthy for sensitive groups, 151–200 red/unhealthy, 201–300 purple/very unhealthy, 301+ maroon/hazardous.
misconceptions: Thinking pollution is only what you can see. Some air pollution (fine particles, ozone) is invisible.
Thinking recycling is the only answer. Reducing and reusing come first because they prevent waste.

days.guide: Explain how air pollution (car exhaust, smoke from wildfires, factories) can irritate lungs and trigger asthma, and how water pollution can make people sick.

questions.q: How can air pollution affect health?
questions.a: It can irritate the lungs, cause coughing and trouble breathing, and trigger asthma attacks.

questions.q: Name two sources of air pollution.
questions.a: Car exhaust, wildfire smoke, factories, power plants, burning trash.

days.guide: Each day, check AirNow for your ZIP code, record the AQI number and color, and decide if it's a good outdoor-play day.

questions.q: The AQI is 160 (red). Should you play hard outside?
questions.a: No. The air is unhealthy for everyone; stay inside or keep outdoor activity light and short.

questions.q: What AQI color is best?
questions.a: Green (0–50), good.

days.guide: With gloves, sort a day's trash into landfill, recycling and compost and weigh each.

questions.q: Which bin does a banana peel go in?
questions.a: Compost.

questions.q: Which bin does a clean plastic bottle go in?
questions.a: Recycling.

days.guide: The family chooses 3 items to reduce, reuse or recycle and writes a plan.

questions.q: What do reduce, reuse and recycle mean?
questions.a: Reduce: use less. Reuse: use things again. Recycle: turn used materials into new products.

days.guide: The child writes the paragraph on how a clean environment keeps people healthy.

questions.q: Why does clean water matter for health?
questions.a: Dirty water can carry germs and chemicals that make people sick.

weeks.assessment_key: AQI log and paragraph key: log has 7 days of AQI values with colors and a correct decision (play outside for green/yellow; limit hard outdoor play at orange for sensitive people; stay inside or keep play light at red or above). Paragraph rubric: 4 = topic sentence, at least 2 specific ways a clean environment protects health (clean air helps breathing/asthma, clean water prevents illness, less trash means fewer germs and pests), a concluding sentence; 3 = 1 specific way; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gloves, trash bags, a clipboard with a tally sheet, grabbers if possible. Choose a safe location. Safety rules: gloves on, don't touch sharp items or needles (tell an adult), stay away from traffic and water edges, wash hands after. Prepare Unit 6 quiz below.
misconceptions: Picking up sharp or dangerous items. Never touch glass shards, needles or chemicals; point them out to an adult.
Thinking one family's cleanup doesn't matter. Data and sharing results can inspire others.

days.guide: Choose a site, list supplies and write 4 safety rules together.

questions.q: What should you do if you find a needle or broken glass?
questions.a: Don't touch it; tell an adult right away.

days.guide: Do the cleanup for 1 hour, tallying items by type (wrappers, bottles, cans, cigarette butts, etc.).

questions.q: Why wear gloves during a cleanup?
questions.a: To protect your hands from germs and sharp objects.

days.guide: The child makes a bar graph of the tallies and identifies the most common item.

questions.q: What does the tallest bar on your graph tell you?
questions.a: The most common type of trash collected.

days.guide: The child writes a short letter or post sharing results and asking others to help.

questions.q: What should your letter include?
questions.a: What you did, what you found (data), why it matters for health, and a request for others to help.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 quiz.

questions.q: How many hours of sleep do kids need?
questions.a: 9–12 hours.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 quiz key: 1) Wash hands for 20 seconds with soap. 2) Sneeze into your elbow. 3) Bacteria vs. viruses: bacteria are single-celled; viruses are smaller and cause colds/flu. 4) Brush 2 minutes twice a day; floss once a day. 5) Kids need 9–12 hours of sleep. 6) Use SPF 30+ sunscreen. 7) A pharmacist prepares and explains medicine. 8) An AQI of 0–50 (green) is good. 9) Reduce, reuse, recycle. 10) Clean environments prevent illness. Graph proficient: bar graph with title, labeled axes, correct tallies, most common item identified. 8–10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Planning sheet with sections: topic, audience, message, 3 facts, materials. Have KidsHealth and MyPlate open for fact-checking.
misconceptions: Choosing a topic too broad ('be healthy'). Narrow to one action, like 'wash your hands for 20 seconds.'
Writing facts from memory without checking. Every fact should come from a reliable source.

days.guide: The child reviews the year's topics and chooses one to promote, explaining why it matters.

questions.q: Why is your chosen topic important?
questions.a: Answer should give a health reason, e.g., 'Helmets prevent head injuries.'

days.guide: Choose an audience and list what they already know and need to know.

questions.q: How would a message for 5-year-olds differ from one for adults?
questions.a: Simpler words, more pictures, shorter sentences and fun elements for young children.

days.guide: Write a positive message (e.g., 'Wash for 20, beat the germs!') with 3 facts.

questions.q: What makes a health message 'positive'?
questions.a: It tells people what to do and the benefit, instead of only scaring them.

days.guide: Plan what goes on the poster, in the brochure and in the PSA.

questions.q: What is a PSA?
questions.a: A public service announcement: a short message to inform the public about something important for their health or safety.

days.guide: Share the plan with you; give 2 compliments and 1 suggestion; the child revises.

questions.q: Is your message clear in one sentence?
questions.a: Yes, it states one action and the benefit.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign plan rubric: 4 = names one specific health topic, a specific audience and what they need, a short positive message, 3 accurate facts with sources, and the 3 planned materials (poster, brochure, 1-minute PSA); revised after parent feedback; 3 = all parts but one fact weak or unsourced; 2 = missing 2 parts; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Poster board, markers, paper for a tri-fold brochure, a phone or tablet for recording.
misconceptions: Putting too much text on a poster. A poster needs a big slogan, a picture and only a few words.
Recording without practicing. Read the script aloud 2–3 times first.

days.guide: The child creates the poster with a catchy slogan and picture.

questions.q: What makes a slogan catchy?
questions.a: It is short, memorable and may rhyme or use rhythm, e.g., 'Buckle up, every trip!'

days.guide: Fold paper into thirds and make a brochure: cover, facts, tips and where to learn more.

questions.q: What goes on the cover of a brochure?
questions.a: The title, a picture and the main message.

days.guide: Write a PSA script: hook, problem, facts, action, slogan. Time it to about 1 minute.

questions.q: What is a 'call to action'?
questions.a: Telling the audience exactly what to do, like 'Wear your helmet every time you ride.'

days.guide: Record the PSA. Allow retakes.

questions.q: What helps a recording sound clear?
questions.a: A quiet room, speaking slowly and loudly, and practicing first.

days.guide: Check each fact against KidsHealth or MyPlate, fix errors, and practice presenting.

questions.q: Why check facts?
questions.a: So the campaign gives true information and people can trust it.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign materials rubric: 4 = poster has a readable slogan and picture; brochure is tri-fold with 3+ accurate facts and tips; PSA script is about 1 minute with a hook, facts and call to action; all facts checked against KidsHealth or MyPlate; 3 = all materials with a minor error; 2 = one material missing or several inaccuracies; 1 = mostly incomplete.

weeks.prep: Campaign materials, an audience (family, cousins, co-op). Prepare the final quiz below.
misconceptions: Thinking a presentation is finished once it's given. Asking for feedback shows whether the message worked.
Setting vague summer goals. Use SMART goals with numbers and times.

days.guide: The child presents the campaign to the chosen audience using the poster, brochure and PSA.

questions.q: What is the one action you want your audience to take?
questions.a: Answer states the campaign's call to action.

days.guide: The child asks the audience what they learned and one change they'll make, and records answers.

questions.q: Why ask for feedback?
questions.a: To find out whether the message was understood and how to improve it.

days.guide: Give the final quiz.

questions.q: How many food groups are on MyPlate?
questions.a: Five.

days.guide: The child sets 2 SMART summer health goals.

questions.q: Make 'sleep better' a SMART goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will be in bed by 8:30 p.m. at least 6 nights a week all summer.'

days.guide: The child writes a reflection on the healthiest change they made this year.

questions.q: What made the change possible?
questions.a: Answer names a strategy or support, such as a tracker, family help or a reminder.

weeks.assessment_key: Final quiz key (12 questions): 1) Five food groups: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy. 2) Kids need 60 minutes of activity a day. 3) On labels, check serving size first. 4) The heart is a muscle that pumps blood. 5) Calcium builds bones. 6) I-message: I feel ___ when ___ because ___. 7) Bullying is repeated, on purpose, with a power imbalance. 8) Fire: get out, stay out, crawl low. 9) 911: name, address, what happened. 10) Only take medicine from a trusted adult. 11) Nicotine is addictive; legal age 21. 12) Wash hands 20 seconds. Presentation rubric: 4 = clear voice, eye contact, accurate facts, all materials, answers questions; 3 = minor issues; 2 = reads everything, little interaction; 1 = incomplete. 10–12 = proficient.
